Graded ring S is Q[x_1,...,x_d] with weighted grading deg(x_i)=B+i for i=1..d
If d=0, interpret S as Q (no variables, hence no f_i witnesses needed)
Each f_i is homogeneous in S with weighted degree deg(f_i)=A+i
Regularity condition: in the successive quotient S/(f_1,...,f_{i-1}), the class of f_i is not a zero-divisor (equivalently: (f_1,...,f_d) is a homogeneous regular sequence in S)
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Let A,B,d ∈ Z with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, and define Q_{A,B,d}(q)=∏_{i=1}^d (1-q^{A+i})/(1-q^{B+i}) with Q_{A,B,0}(q)=1. If Q_{A,B,d}(q) ∈ Q[q], then in the weighted graded polynomial ring S=Q[x_1,...,x_d] (or S=Q if d=0) with deg(x_i)=B+i, there exist homogeneous elements f_1,...,f_d ∈ S such that deg(f_i)=A+i for each i=1..d and for each i the class of f_i in S/(f_1,...,f_{i-1}) is not a zero-divisor (so f_1,...,f_d form a homogeneous regular sequence). Consequently, the graded data of S modulo this regular sequence yields the given expression Q_{A,B,d}(q) (as stated in the equivalence).

ancestry_summary.statement_nl: For integers A, B, d with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, define Q_{A,B,d}(q) := prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)), with the empty product equal to 1 when d = 0. Assume Q_{A,B,d}(q) belongs to Q[q]. Let S be the weighted polynomial ring Q[x_1, ..., x_d] graded by deg(x_i) = B+i; when d = 0 interpret S as Q. Then there exist homogeneous polynomials f_1, ..., f_d in S such that deg(f_i) = A+i for every i, and for each i the image of f_i in S/(f_1, ..., f_{i-1}) is not a zero-divisor. Equivalently, Q_{A,B,d}(q) is realized by a homogeneous regular sequence in a weighted polynomial ring with variable weights B+1, ..., B+d and relation degrees A+1, ..., A+d.

ancestry_summary.statement_nl: Let [n choose k]_q denote the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient. Prove that for all integers n, k, l with 0 ≤ k, l ≤ n, if [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q is a polynomial in q, then that polynomial has only nonnegative coefficients.

payload.proof_nl:
Set N(q)=prod_{i=1}^d (1-q^(A+i)) and D(q)=prod_{i=1}^d (1-q^(B+i)), so the given rational function is N(q)/D(q).

Because N and D are polynomials with rational coefficients and D != 0, the condition N(q)/D(q) in Q[q] is equivalent to D dividing N in the rational-coefficient polynomial ring. We may test this after extending coefficients to the complex numbers: if D divides N over the rationals, then certainly D divides N over the complexes. Conversely, suppose N=D P with P a complex-coefficient polynomial. Divide N by D in the rational-coefficient polynomial ring: N=D Q0+R with Q0,R having rational coefficients and either R=0 or deg R < deg D. Then R=D(P-Q0). If R != 0, then deg R = deg D + deg(P-Q0) >= deg D, contradiction. Hence R=0, so D already divides N over the rationals.

Now work over the complex numbers. For alpha in C and nonzero F, let nu_alpha(F) be the multiplicity of alpha as a root of F. Since every complex polynomial factors into linear factors, and nonzero constants are units, D divides N over the complexes if and only if nu_alpha(D) <= nu_alpha(N) for every complex number alpha.

Fix alpha in C. If alpha is not a root of unity, then alpha^m != 1 for every positive integer m, so nu_alpha(1-q^m)=0 for all m. If alpha has exact order n, then for every positive integer m,
nu_alpha(1-q^m)=1 when n divides m, and 0 otherwise.
Indeed, alpha is a root exactly when alpha^m=1, which is equivalent to n dividing m. In that case the root is simple, because the derivative of 1-q^m is -m q^(m-1), and at q=alpha this equals -m alpha^(m-1) != 0.

Therefore, for alpha of exact order n, multiplicities add over products, so
nu_alpha(D)=sum_{i=1}^d nu_alpha(1-q^(B+i)) = #{ i in {1,...,d} : n divides B+i } = mu_n(B,d),
and similarly
nu_alpha(N)=mu_n(A,d).
If alpha is not a root of unity, both multiplicities are 0.

Hence D divides N over the complexes if and only if for every root of unity alpha of exact order n we have mu_n(B,d) <= mu_n(A,d). Since for each positive integer n there exists a complex number of exact order n, for example exp(2 pi i / n), this is equivalent to requiring mu_n(B,d) <= mu_n(A,d) for every positive integer n.

Combining this with the first paragraph, the rational function Q(q) belongs to Q[q] if and only if mu_n(B,d) <= mu_n(A,d) for every positive integer n. This is exactly the statement.

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For fixed integers A and B and nonnegative integer d satisfying A >= B >= 0, define Q(q) as the product over i from 1 to d of (1 minus q to the power (A plus i)) divided by (1 minus q to the power (B plus i)), with the convention that when d = 0 the product equals 1. For each positive integer n and integer C define mu_n(C,d) as the number of i in {1, ..., d} such that n divides C plus i. Then Q(q) is a polynomial in q with rational coefficients (belongs to Q[q]) if and only if for every positive integer n, mu_n(B,d) is at most mu_n(A,d).
quantifier_order: Let A, B, d be integers with constraints A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0.
Define Q(q) using the product from i = 1 to d, with the empty product equal to 1 when d = 0.
Define mu_n(C,d) for each positive integer n.
Claim: Q(q) is in Q[q] if and only if for every positive integer n, mu_n(B,d) is <= mu_n(A,d).

payload.statement_nl: Let A,B,d be integers with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, and define Q(q) := prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)), with the empty product equal to 1 if d=0. For each positive integer n define mu_n(C,d) := #{ i in {1,...,d} : n divides C+i }. Then Q(q) belongs to Q[q] if and only if mu_n(B,d) <= mu_n(A,d) for every positive integer n.

detailed_findings.finding: The reduction from Q(q) in Q[q] to divisibility D | N in Q[q], and the transfer of divisibility between Q and C, is mathematically sound.

The root-multiplicity analysis is correct: 1-q^m has a simple root at alpha exactly when alpha is a root of unity with order dividing m, so the multiplicities in N and D are exactly the counting functions mu_n(A,d) and mu_n(B,d).

result_payload.reason: The proof gives a complete equivalence. It correctly reduces polynomiality of N/D to divisibility D | N in Q[q], justifies that divisibility over Q is equivalent to divisibility over C, and then characterizes divisibility over C by comparing root multiplicities at every complex number. The multiplicity of a factor 1-q^m at a complex number alpha is correctly shown to be 1 exactly when alpha is a root of unity whose order divides m, and 0 otherwise; summing these multiplicities over the product gives precisely mu_n(B,d) and mu_n(A,d). Since primitive n-th roots exist for every positive integer n, this yields the claimed iff criterion. No undeclared or forbidden dependencies are used.
